articles.0.title: What is Carbon Intensity and Why It Matters
articles.0.summary: Carbon intensity compares lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions per unit of energy. The boundary, method, and supporting evidence matter as much as the number.
articles.0.content:
Carbon intensity (CI) expresses greenhouse gas emissions per unit of energy, usually in grams of CO₂ equivalent per megajoule (gCO₂e/MJ). A CI number is comparable only when the lifecycle boundary, gases, global-warming potentials, calorific-value basis, and calculation method are also comparable. It is not a complete sustainability score.

The International Maritime Organization's 2024 lifecycle guidelines separate well-to-tank emissions from tank-to-wake emissions and combine them for a well-to-wake result. Feedstock, production energy, transport, fuel pathway, and onboard conversion can all affect that result. A fuel name alone therefore does not establish its lifecycle CI.

FuelEU Maritime uses a defined well-to-wake method for the yearly average GHG intensity of energy used on board an in-scope ship. Its reference value is 91.16 gCO₂e/MJ, reduced by 2% for 2025 through 2029, which is 89.34 gCO₂e/MJ when rounded to two decimals. The EU ETS is a separate system: a shipping company surrenders allowances for reported emissions that fall within ETS scope. It does not calculate that obligation directly from a quoted lifecycle CI value.

For procurement, ask which boundary and method produced the number, whether the value is a default or an actual value, which evidence supports the feedstock and pathway, who verified it, and for what period it is valid. Also check that the energy basis and units match before comparing offers.

Verdaxis records supplier-declared CI on executable ASK listings and records a declared lifecycle method for B30 and B100 listings. These fields help buyers compare declarations. Verdaxis does not independently verify supplier certificates or the declared CI, so buyers must review the supporting documents and the rules that apply to their use case.
articles.0.references.0: IMO Resolution MEPC.391(81): 2024 lifecycle GHG guidelines
articles.1.title: Physical vs Book & Claim
articles.1.summary: Physical chain of custody and Book & Claim connect fuel and environmental attributes in different ways. The governing scheme determines what evidence and claims are valid.
articles.1.content:
A physical chain-of-custody model keeps certified material or its sustainability characteristics connected to a physical supply chain. The exact connection depends on the scheme. Identity-preserved, segregated, and mass-balance models do not provide the same level of physical separation, so the model and its records must be named.

Book & Claim separates defined sustainability attributes from delivery of the physical fuel. The RSB Book & Claim Manual, for example, sets rules for eligible certified product, registration, transfer, and retirement of Book & Claim Units. A unit has meaning within that system because the manual, registry, account controls, and audit requirements define who may issue it and what the holder may claim.

A credible Book & Claim review should confirm the issuing scheme, eligible product and quantity, unique registry record, transfer history, retirement status, permitted claim wording, and safeguards against duplicate issuance or use. A certificate or spreadsheet outside those controls is not equivalent to a registry retirement statement.

Regulatory acceptance is a separate question. Whether an instrument supports FuelEU Maritime, another regulation, or a corporate disclosure depends on that rule and the evidence accepted by the relevant verifier or authority. A Book & Claim record should not be described as regulatory compliance unless the governing rule permits that use.

Verdaxis currently operates an order book for physical fuel bids and asks with supplier-declared product and sustainability fields. It does not issue, transfer, or retire Book & Claim units, and it does not check an external Book & Claim registry. A Verdaxis listing or trade record is therefore not evidence that an environmental attribute was retired.
articles.2.title: Why Compliance is Not the Same as Credits
articles.2.summary: FuelEU compliance balances, EU ETS allowances, and voluntary carbon credits are different instruments. Each can be used only for the purpose allowed by its governing rules.
articles.2.content:
A compliance obligation is created by a law or regulation and is met through the mechanisms that rule permits. A voluntary carbon credit is issued under a separate voluntary programme. Similar climate terminology does not make the instruments interchangeable.

FuelEU Maritime calculates a compliance balance for each in-scope ship and provides defined flexibility through banking, borrowing, and pooling, subject to the regulation's conditions. The EU ETS requires shipping companies to surrender EU allowances for the share of verified emissions covered by the scheme. A voluntary carbon credit is not a FuelEU compliance balance or an EU allowance.

A company may use voluntary credits for a separate voluntary claim if the chosen standard allows it. That use does not change the ship's FuelEU calculation or remove its EU ETS surrender obligation. Reports should identify the programme, vintage, retirement record, claim boundary, and whether the credit is presented separately from gross emissions and regulatory compliance.

Fuel buyers should identify the obligation first, then check the accepted instrument, responsible entity, reporting period, verifier, deadline, and evidence. This avoids treating a fuel declaration, an allowance, a compliance balance, and a voluntary credit as if they were the same asset.

The current Verdaxis marketplace lists physical marine-fuel products, not voluntary carbon credits. Supplier certification and CI fields are declarations used in the trading workflow. They do not by themselves establish that a buyer has met FuelEU Maritime, EU ETS, or another legal obligation.

articles.3.title: How to Account for Scope 3 Fuel Emissions Carefully
articles.3.summary: Scope 3 fuel accounting starts with the reporting boundary and a consistent method. Supplier data can improve an estimate, but a transaction record is not an assured emissions inventory.
articles.3.content:
Scope 3 covers indirect value-chain emissions that are outside a reporting company's Scope 1 and Scope 2 boundary. Under the GHG Protocol, upstream emissions from purchased fuels can fall in Category 3, while combustion on a vessel owned or controlled by the reporting company is normally Scope 1. Charter and lease arrangements can change the classification, so the company's consolidation approach must be set before the calculation.

The GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard permits calculation with activity data and emission factors, including estimates where primary data is unavailable. IFRS S2 also requires disclosure of the measurement approach, inputs, and assumptions used for Scope 3. More specific supplier data can be useful, but only when its lifecycle boundary, gases, global-warming potentials, allocation method, units, and reporting period fit the inventory method.

A supplier's lifecycle CI should not be copied into a corporate inventory without reconciliation. Multiply only compatible activity data and factors, keep well-to-tank and tank-to-wake boundaries clear, document exclusions, and retain the source and version of each factor. Report significant estimation uncertainty rather than presenting a modelled value as direct measurement.

Scope 3 inventories of different companies can overlap by design because one company's direct emissions can appear in another company's value chain. That overlap does not by itself prove an error. The reporting company should prevent duplicate entries within its own inventory and should not claim exclusive ownership of a reduction unless the applicable claim standard and evidence support that statement.

Verdaxis records supplier-declared CI, method, feedstock, origin, and certification fields for relevant listings. It does not currently prepare a company's Scope 3 inventory, retire environmental attributes, or provide assurance over those declarations. Use the platform record as a commercial data input and review the underlying evidence before using it in a report or reduction claim.

articles.4.title: Energy Content Matters: Why $/Tonne Isn't Enough
articles.4.summary: A price per tonne can hide differences in delivered energy. Converting offers to a common energy basis makes the assumptions and trade-offs visible.
articles.4.content:
Marine fuel is commonly quoted by mass, but propulsion depends on usable energy. Lower calorific value (LCV) is often expressed in MJ/kg. Numerically, 1 MJ/kg equals 1 GJ per metric tonne, so an energy-basis comparison can divide the price per tonne by the LCV to estimate price per GJ.

For an illustration only, assume two offers both cost USD 600 per tonne. At 40.5 MJ/kg, the energy price is about USD 14.81/GJ. At 42.7 MJ/kg, it is about USD 14.05/GJ. The first offer is about 5.4% more expensive per unit of stated energy. These are explicit calculation assumptions, not current market quotes or evidence about a particular fuel lot.

The calculation is only a first comparison. Confirm whether values use LCV or higher calorific value, use a consistent laboratory or regulatory method, and consider engine efficiency, fuel quality, handling losses, and any operational limits. A declared or default energy value is not the same as a tested batch result.

Energy content and greenhouse gas performance must also stay separate. FuelEU Maritime combines energy use with prescribed well-to-wake emission factors and other rules. The EU ETS applies to covered reported emissions. A lower price per GJ does not prove lower lifecycle emissions, regulatory eligibility, or a lower total compliance cost.

The Verdaxis public energy calculator lets a user enter price, energy density, consumption, voyage, allowance-price, and coverage assumptions. Its price-per-GJ and voyage results are scenarios based on those inputs. They are not supplier quotes, verified laboratory results, or compliance determinations.

articles.5.title: FuelEU Maritime: What Fuel Buyers Need to Know
articles.5.summary: FuelEU Maritime has applied since 1 January 2025. It limits the yearly well-to-wake GHG intensity of energy used by ships within its scope.
articles.5.content:
FuelEU Maritime has applied since 1 January 2025. It covers ships above 5,000 gross tonnage that transport passengers or cargo for commercial purposes, regardless of flag, subject to the exclusions and special provisions in Article 2. Within that scope, the calculation generally covers 100% of energy used on voyages between covered EU ports and within a covered EU port, and 50% on voyages between a covered EU port and a third-country port.

The regulation starts from a reference value of 91.16 gCO₂e/MJ. The limit is reduced by 2% from 2025 through 2029, giving 89.34 gCO₂e/MJ when rounded to two decimals. The reduction becomes 6% in 2030, 14.5% in 2035, 31% in 2040, 62% in 2045, and 80% in 2050.

Compliance is assessed for each reporting period using the yearly average well-to-wake GHG intensity of energy used on board. The calculation follows the regulation's method and prescribed factors, and reported data is checked by an accredited verifier. A commercial fuel label or supplier CI declaration does not replace that process.

The regulation allows banking of a surplus, limited borrowing of an advance surplus, and pooling between ships when its conditions are met. A pool must have a positive total compliance balance; allocation cannot make a deficient ship more deficient or turn a ship with a surplus into a deficient ship. These mechanisms are regulated accounting flexibilities; they should not be described as an unrestricted carbon-credit market.

After annual verification and any permitted banking, borrowing, or pooling, a remaining deficit results in the statutory FuelEU penalty calculated under Annex IV. Repeated deficits increase the penalty multiplier. The actual outcome depends on verified energy use, factors, scope, and any valid flexibility, so a headline fuel price or CI number cannot determine the result alone.

For procurement, collect the fuel pathway, feedstock, well-to-tank and tank-to-wake factors, LCV, quantity, proof of sustainability where required, and the evidence needed by the verifier. Verdaxis tools can compare declared inputs and model planning scenarios. They do not create the official FuelEU report or determine a ship's legal compliance.
